{{short description|Polygon with 1 million edges}}
{{About|a polygon|megaton(ne)|Ton|and|Tonne}}
{{distinguish|Megatron|Steinhaus–Moser notation#Special values}}
{{Regular polygon db|Regular polygon stat table|p1000000}}

A '''megagon''' or '''1,000,000-gon''' (million-gon) is a [[circle]]-like [[polygon]] with [[one million]] sides ([[mega-]], from the Greek μέγας, meaning "great", being a unit prefix denoting a factor of one million).<ref name=Darling/><ref>{{Cite book |last=Dugopolski |first=Mark |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=l8tWAAAAYAAJ |title=College Algebra and Trigonometry |date=1999 |publisher=Addison-Wesley |isbn=978-0-201-34712-8 |pages=505 |language=en}}</ref>

==Regular megagon==
A [[Regular polygon|regular]] megagon is represented by the [[Schläfli symbol]] {1,000,000} and can be constructed as a [[Truncation (geometry)|truncated]] 500,000-gon, t{500,000}, a twice-truncated 250,000-gon, tt{250,000}, a thrice-truncated 125,000-gon, ttt{125,000}, or a four-fold-truncated 62,500-gon, tttt{62,500}, a five-fold-truncated 31,250-gon, {{not a typo|ttttt{31,250}}}, or a six-fold-truncated 15,625-gon, {{not a typo|tttttt{15,625}}}.

A [[regular polygon|regular]] megagon has an interior angle of 179°59'58.704" or
3.14158637 radians.<ref name="Darling">{{Cite book |last=Darling |first=David |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=0YiXM-x--4wC&q=polygon+megagon |title=The Universal Book of Mathematics: From Abracadabra to Zeno's Paradoxes |date=2004-10-28 |publisher=Wiley |isbn=978-0-471-66700-1 |pages=249 |language=en}}</ref> The [[area]] of a [[regular polygon|regular]] megagon with sides of length ''a'' is given by
:<math>A = 250,000 \ a^2 \cot \frac{\pi}{1,000,000}.</math>

The [[perimeter]] of a regular megagon inscribed in the unit [[circle]] is:
:<math>2,000,000 \ \sin\frac{\pi}{1,000,000},</math>
which is exceedingly close to [[2π]]. In fact, for a circle the size of the [[Earth]]'s equator, with a [[circumference]] of 40,075 kilometres, one edge of a megagon inscribed in such a circle would be slightly over 40 meters long. The difference between the perimeter of the inscribed megagon and the circumference of this circle comes to less than 1/16 millimeters.<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=E72yNz5sBY0C&pg=PA45 |title=An Elementary Treatise on the Differential Calculus |publisher=Forgotten Books |isbn=978-1-4400-6681-8 |pages=45 |language=en}}</ref>

Because 1,000,000 = 2<sup>6</sup> &times; 5<sup>6</sup>, the number of sides is not a product of distinct [[Fermat prime]]s and a power of two. Thus the regular megagon is not a [[constructible polygon]]. Indeed, it is not even constructible with the use of an angle trisector, as the number of sides is neither a product of distinct [[Pierpont prime]]s, nor a product of powers of two and three.

==Philosophical application==
Like [[René Descartes]]'s example of the [[chiliagon]], the million-sided polygon has been used as an illustration of a well-defined concept that cannot be visualised.<ref>{{Cite book |last=McCormick |first=John Francis |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=KyFHAAAAIAAJ&q=%22million-sided+polygon%22 |title=Scholastic Metaphysics: Being, its division and causes |date=1928 |publisher=Loyola University Press |pages=18 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Merrill |first=John Calhoun |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_aNZAAAAMAAJ&q=%22million-sided+polygon%22 |title=Philosophy and Journalism |last2=Odell |first2=S. Jack |date=1983 |publisher=Longman |isbn=978-0-582-28157-8 |pages=47 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Hospers |first=John |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=OVu0CORmhL4C&pg=PA56 |title=An Introduction to Philosophical Analysis |date=1997 |publisher=Psychology Press |isbn=978-0-415-15792-6 |edition=4 |pages=56 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Mandik |first=Pete |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=5yHtsM-NToYC&pg=PA26 |title=Key Terms in Philosophy of Mind |date=2010-05-13 |publisher=A&C Black |isbn=978-1-84706-349-6 |pages=26 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Kenny |first=Anthony |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ehZGIy_ZYTgC&pg=PA124 |title=The Rise of Modern Philosophy: A New History of Western Philosophy |date=2006-06-29 |publisher=OUP Oxford |isbn=978-0-19-875277-6 |pages=124 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Balmes |first=Jaime Luciano |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=MrwKHqw06hMC&pg=PA27 |title=Fundamental Philosophy |date=1856 |publisher=Sadlier |pages=27 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Potter |first=Vincent G. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=SnO1FKnJui4C&pg=PA86 |title=On Understanding Understanding: A Philosophy of Knowledge |date=1994 |publisher=Fordham University Press |isbn=978-0-8232-1486-0 |pages=86 |language=en}}</ref>

The megagon is also used as an illustration of the convergence of regular polygons to a circle.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Russell |first=Bertrand |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Ey94E3sOMA0C&pg=PA202 |title=History of Western Philosophy |date=2004 |publisher=Psychology Press |isbn=978-0-415-32505-9 |pages=202 |language=en}}</ref>

==Symmetry==
The ''regular megagon'' has Dih<sub>1,000,000</sub> [[dihedral symmetry]], order 2,000,000, represented by 1,000,000 lines of reflection. Dih<sub>1,000,000</sub> has 48 dihedral subgroups: (Dih<sub>500,000</sub>, Dih<sub>250,000</sub>, Dih<sub>125,000</sub>, Dih<sub>62,500</sub>, Dih<sub>31,250</sub>, Dih<sub>15,625</sub>), (Dih<sub>200,000</sub>, Dih<sub>100,000</sub>, Dih<sub>50,000</sub>, Dih<sub>25,000</sub>, Dih<sub>12,500</sub>, Dih<sub>6,250</sub>, Dih<sub>3,125</sub>), (Dih<sub>40,000</sub>, Dih<sub>20,000</sub>, Dih<sub>10,000</sub>, Dih<sub>5,000</sub>, Dih<sub>2,500</sub>, Dih<sub>1,250</sub>, Dih<sub>625</sub>), (Dih<sub>8,000</sub>, Dih<sub>4,000</sub>, Dih<sub>2,000</sub>, Dih<sub>1,000</sub>, Dih<sub>500</sub>, Dih<sub>250</sub>, Dih<sub>125</sub>, Dih<sub>1,600</sub>, Dih<sub>800</sub>, Dih<sub>400</sub>, Dih<sub>200</sub>, Dih<sub>100</sub>, Dih<sub>50</sub>, Dih<sub>25</sub>), (Dih<sub>320</sub>, Dih<sub>160</sub>, Dih<sub>80</sub>, Dih<sub>40</sub>, Dih<sub>20</sub>, Dih<sub>10</sub>, Dih<sub>5</sub>), and (Dih<sub>64</sub>, Dih<sub>32</sub>, Dih<sub>16</sub>, Dih<sub>8</sub>, Dih<sub>4</sub>, Dih<sub>2</sub>, Dih<sub>1</sub>). It also has 49 more [[cyclic group|cyclic]] symmetries as subgroups: (Z<sub>1,000,000</sub>, Z<sub>500,000</sub>, Z<sub>250,000</sub>, Z<sub>125,000</sub>, Z<sub>62,500</sub>, Z<sub>31,250</sub>, Z<sub>15,625</sub>), (Z<sub>200,000</sub>, Z<sub>100,000</sub>, Z<sub>50,000</sub>, Z<sub>25,000</sub>, Z<sub>12,500</sub>, Z<sub>6,250</sub>, Z<sub>3,125</sub>), (Z<sub>40,000</sub>, Z<sub>20,000</sub>, Z<sub>10,000</sub>, Z<sub>5,000</sub>, Z<sub>2,500</sub>, Z<sub>1,250</sub>, Z<sub>625</sub>), (Z<sub>8,000</sub>, Z<sub>4,000</sub>, Z<sub>2,000</sub>, Z<sub>1,000</sub>, Z<sub>500</sub>, Z<sub>250</sub>, Z<sub>125</sub>), (Z<sub>1,600</sub>, Z<sub>800</sub>, Z<sub>400</sub>, Z<sub>200</sub>, Z<sub>100</sub>, Z<sub>50</sub>, Z<sub>25</sub>), (Z<sub>320</sub>, Z<sub>160</sub>, Z<sub>80</sub>, Z<sub>40</sub>, Z<sub>20</sub>, Z<sub>10</sub>, Z<sub>5</sub>), and (Z<sub>64</sub>, Z<sub>32</sub>, Z<sub>16</sub>, Z<sub>8</sub>, Z<sub>4</sub>, Z<sub>2</sub>, Z<sub>1</sub>), with Z<sub>n</sub> representing &pi;/''n'' radian rotational symmetry.

[[John Horton Conway|John Conway]] labeled these lower symmetries with a letter and order of the symmetry follows the letter.<ref>'''The Symmetries of Things''', Chapter 20</ref> '''r2000000''' represents full symmetry and '''a1''' labels no symmetry. He gives '''d''' (diagonal) with mirror lines through vertices, '''p''' with mirror lines through edges (perpendicular), '''i''' with mirror lines through both vertices and edges, and '''g''' for rotational symmetry. 

These lower symmetries allows degrees of freedom in defining irregular megagons. Only the '''g1000000''' subgroup has no degrees of freedom but can be seen as [[directed edge]]s.

==Megagram==
A megagram is a million-sided [[star polygon]]. There are 199,999 regular forms{{efn|content=199,999 = 500,000 cases − 1 (convex) − 100,000 (multiples of 5) − 250,000 (multiples of 2) + 50,000 (multiples of 2 and 5)}} given by [[Schläfli symbol]]s of the form {1000000/''n''}, where ''n'' is an integer between 2 and 500,000 that is [[coprime]] to 1,000,000. There are also 300,000 regular [[star figure]]s in the remaining cases.
